legal_status_note: These are realistic, synthetic training scenarios, not reports of actual organisations or incidents. Monetary amounts are statutory ceilings, not predictions or automatic penalties. Check the notified text, commencement notifications, corrigenda and applicable sectoral law before operational legal use.

cases.title: Telemedicine Patient Data Breach and Ransomware
cases.scenario_background: A telemedicine provider stores patient profiles, prescriptions, consultation notes and appointment records in a cloud platform. Attackers compromise a privileged support credential, exfiltrate files and encrypt part of the environment. The service uses a cloud processor; MFA coverage is incomplete, database audit logs are fragmented, and the organisation has not yet established the full incident timeline.
facts: The affected dataset contains sensitive health-related personal information, although the Act does not create a separate statutory sensitive-data category.
A privileged account was used to access and export records.
The processor detected suspicious activity before the Data Fiduciary completed its own assessment.
Some backups exist, but restoration and integrity checks have not been tested recently.
The organisation must establish scope, containment, notification duties and other applicable health-sector obligations.
legal_issues: Section 8(1): the Data Fiduciary remains responsible for processing undertaken on its behalf.
Sections 8(2) and 8(5): processor engagement must be under a valid contract; reasonable security safeguards are required.
Section 8(6) and Rule 7: assess and make the prescribed breach intimations; Rule 7 has phased commencement.
Rule 6: assess the notified security safeguard measures, including access controls, logging/monitoring, continuity, processor terms and relevant log retention. Rule 6 has phased commencement.
Check current commencement and any applicable health-sector, CERT-In or other legal duties separately.
penalty_analysis: Act Schedule, entry 1
Failure to take reasonable security safeguards under Section 8(5)
Up to ₹250 crore
Maximum statutory ceiling; establish the contravention, commencement and facts. Not an automatic incident fine.
Act Schedule, entry 2
Failure to give required breach intimation under Section 8(6)
Up to ₹200 crore
Separate exposure only if the applicable notification duty is breached; assess current commencement and Rule 7 timing.
remediation: Contain compromised credentials and preserve forensic evidence before routine log rotation or system rebuilds.
Determine affected systems, data categories, access window, exfiltration evidence and Data Principals; record unknowns and investigation owners.
Apply strong authentication, least-privilege access, privileged-session monitoring and time-limited support access.
Centralise protected audit logs, alert on unusual bulk access/export, and test incident escalation with the processor.
Restore from verified backups and test data integrity and service continuity.
Make a documented notification assessment against the operative Act/Rules and all independently applicable sectoral deadlines.
cases.remediation_strategy: Use an incident command process that separates containment, forensic fact-finding, legal notification analysis, service restoration and processor oversight. Track each action to dated evidence.
questions: Which facts must be confirmed before the notification decision?
Why does using a cloud processor not remove the Data Fiduciary's accountability?
Which Rule 6 controls address prevention, detection and continuity?

cases.title: Fintech App: Unbundled Consent and Cross-Border Access
cases.scenario_background: A payments app presents one mandatory 'Accept all' button for account servicing, behavioural analytics and promotional offers. Withdrawal is buried in support pages. An overseas support vendor can view customer profiles and transaction metadata, while backups are replicated to a foreign region. Procurement has not mapped all subprocessors or destinations.
facts: Service-essential and optional marketing/analytics purposes are bundled in one interface.
The user journey makes refusal and later withdrawal materially harder than acceptance.
The CRM and analytics processor may retain stale consent state after withdrawal.
Foreign support access and backup replication are not captured in the transfer inventory.
Financial-sector directions and restrictions must be assessed independently; an overseas destination alone does not prove a DPDPA contravention.
legal_issues: Sections 5-6: notice and consent lifecycle, including specific purposes and withdrawal that is as easy as giving consent.
Rule 3: prescribed notice detail, subject to its commencement date.
Sections 8(1)-(2): Data Fiduciary accountability and processor-contract governance.
Section 16 and Rule 15: assess any Government transfer restriction and relevant sectoral conditions; neither creates a blanket localisation rule by itself.
Rule 14: Data Principal rights workflow, subject to phased commencement.
penalty_analysis: Act Schedule, entry 7
Any other established contravention of the Act or Rules, including applicable notice/consent obligations
Up to ₹50 crore
Catch-all ceiling only; identify the precise contravention and operative provision. No penalty follows merely from optional analytics or overseas access without the legal analysis.
remediation: Separate account-service processing from genuinely optional analytics and marketing choices.
Give a purpose-specific notice and affirmative, granular choice; do not make optional consent a condition of unrelated service access.
Provide withdrawal with comparable ease, propagate it to every processor and suppress future use for that purpose.
Inventory remote access, storage, backups and subprocessors, then assess current Section 16 restrictions and financial-sector rules.
Use least-privilege, just-in-time overseas support access and retain access evidence.
Test consent capture, withdrawal propagation and transfer controls end to end.
cases.remediation_strategy: Treat consent UX and cross-border processing as separate workstreams: product teams remediate purpose choice and withdrawal, while privacy/security/procurement jointly map and approve destinations and vendor access.
questions: Which purposes should be separated in the user interface?
What records prove that withdrawal reached downstream processors?
Why is overseas access not, by itself, proof of a Section 16 breach?

cases.title: E-Commerce Dark Patterns and Consent Withdrawal Friction
cases.scenario_background: An online marketplace uses a prominent 'Accept all' control and a low-contrast settings link for optional targeted advertising. Turning off marketing requires several screens, while signing up takes one click. After a customer withdraws, a connected CRM continues promotional messages because it holds a stale consent flag.
facts: Account servicing and marketing are different processing purposes.
Optional advertising consent is presented in a visually coercive, bundled interface.
Withdrawal requires materially more effort than giving consent.
A downstream CRM continues messages after withdrawal.
A user-interface dark pattern is evidence of design friction; determine the applicable statutory contravention rather than assuming that every interface issue maps to a separate DPDP penalty.
legal_issues: Sections 5-6: clear notice, specific consent and withdrawal as easy as giving consent.
Section 8(1)-(2): accountability for downstream processing and processor arrangements.
Rule 3: notice content requirements, subject to commencement.
Section 13 and Rule 14: an accessible grievance path and rights workflow; Rule 14 has phased commencement.
Assess consumer-protection dark-pattern rules separately where applicable.
penalty_analysis: Act Schedule, entry 7
Any other established contravention, potentially including applicable notice/consent or rights duties
Up to ₹50 crore
Maximum, not automatic. Identify the breached provision and operative rule; consumer-protection consequences are a separate analysis.
remediation: Redesign the interface so optional purposes are separately and neutrally presented.
Make withdrawal discoverable and no harder than granting consent.
Use a central purpose-level consent state and block sends at execution time if consent is absent or withdrawn.
Propagate revocation events to CRM, advertising and analytics vendors with retry and reconciliation.
Maintain versioned notices, consent/withdrawal timestamps and user-journey test evidence.
Run usability tests for refusal and withdrawal, and route unresolved complaints through the published grievance process.
cases.remediation_strategy: Pair a design review with system-level tests: measure clicks/time for consent and withdrawal, then verify no downstream campaign executes after revocation.
questions: How does the interface make withdrawal harder than giving consent?
Which test proves the CRM no longer sends after revocation?
What is the difference between a statutory maximum and an automatic penalty?

cases.title: EdTech Children's Data Tracking and Targeted Advertising
cases.scenario_background: A learning platform serves school-age users and records lesson activity, assessment results and device events. A marketing SDK receives behavioural signals for ad targeting. The service can identify users under 18, but guardian verification is incomplete and the product team has not documented whether a statutory exemption applies.
facts: The platform processes personal data of users who may be children under the Act.
Behavioural events are shared with an advertising SDK.
The guardian-consent workflow has not been tested for identity and age verification.
No documented statutory exemption analysis exists.
Learning analytics needed to provide the service must be distinguished from behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising.
legal_issues: Section 9: verifiable consent and restrictions on processing children's personal data, subject to statutory exemptions.
Rules 10-12 and the Fourth Schedule: verification and specified exemptions, subject to commencement and conditions.
Sections 8(1)-(2): Data Fiduciary accountability and processor governance.
Section 33 and the Act Schedule, entry 3: maximum penalty for failure to fulfil additional child-data obligations.
penalty_analysis: Act Schedule, entry 3
Failure to fulfil additional obligations relating to children's personal data under Section 9
Up to ₹200 crore
Maximum statutory ceiling; establish applicability, the exact duty, any valid exemption and commencement. Not automatic.
remediation: Disable targeted advertising and unnecessary behavioural monitoring for child accounts pending a documented legal assessment.
Map all SDK events and stop collection or sharing not needed for the specified service purpose.
Implement age/guardian verification and verifiable consent where required by the operative provisions.
Assess every claimed exemption against its class, conditions, safeguards and current commencement.
Contractually restrict vendor use and prohibit secondary advertising use.
Test the child-account experience, consent records, SDK allowlist and deletion/withdrawal propagation.
cases.remediation_strategy: Make child status a protected policy signal enforced at collection and egress boundaries. Require privacy/legal approval and auditable exemption evidence before enabling any exception.
questions: Why is ordinary user acceptance not enough to prove verifiable parental consent?
What must be established before relying on an exemption?
Which data flow must be disabled while advertising use is reviewed?

cases.title: IT/ITES BPO Vendor Breach: Fiduciary and Processor Responsibilities
cases.scenario_background: An Indian business outsources customer-support operations to an IT/ITES BPO. The vendor's staff use a shared account to access customer profiles, and an unapproved subprocessor stores call recordings. A compromised vendor laptop exposes a batch of records. The master services agreement contains general confidentiality language but no tested incident escalation or specific security schedule.
facts: The organisation determines why customer records are processed; the BPO acts on its behalf for defined support tasks.
Shared accounts prevent reliable attribution of access.
A subprocessor was introduced without the organisation's approval or a complete data-flow assessment.
The Data Fiduciary learned of the incident after the processor's initial detection.
The processor's operational role does not erase the Data Fiduciary's statutory responsibilities.
legal_issues: Sections 8(1)-(2): Data Fiduciary responsibility for processing on its behalf and engagement of processors under a valid contract.
Sections 8(5)-(6): security safeguards and breach intimation duties.
Rules 6-7: security and breach-intimation details, subject to phased commencement.
The Act's definition of Data Processor turns on processing on behalf of a Data Fiduciary; contractual labels do not override actual roles.
penalty_analysis: Act Schedule, entry 1
Failure by the Data Fiduciary to take reasonable security safeguards under Section 8(5)
Up to ₹250 crore
Potential ceiling if the contravention is established; outsourcing does not automatically avoid the Data Fiduciary's accountability.
Act Schedule, entry 2
Failure to give required breach intimation under Section 8(6)
Up to ₹200 crore
Assess the Data Fiduciary's own notification conduct and applicable commencement; the processor incident alone does not prove this contravention.
Act Schedule, entry 7
Other established contravention, such as an applicable processor-contract duty
Up to ₹50 crore
Apply only after identifying the exact breached provision; do not stack maxima mechanically.
remediation: Contain compromised devices and accounts; preserve endpoint, identity, call-recording and subprocessor evidence.
Replace shared accounts with named identities, least privilege and monitored privileged access.
Map every subprocessor and processing location; require approval, flow-down controls and evidence.
Replace generic confidentiality wording with a contract schedule covering security, incident escalation, access, retention, deletion and audit support.
Set an immediate processor-to-fiduciary escalation path and run a joint breach tabletop.
The Data Fiduciary should independently assess affected Data Principals, statutory notifications and remediation rather than waiting for the vendor to decide.
cases.remediation_strategy: Use an evidence-based role and contract review: confirm who determines purposes and means, then map each processor/subprocessor to permitted instructions, controls, incident duties and verification evidence.
questions: Which party remains responsible under Section 8(1) for processing undertaken on its behalf?
What contract and technical evidence should the controller require?
Why do contractual role labels not replace analysis of actual processing?

cases.title: Employee HR Data and the Boundaries of Section 7
cases.scenario_background: An employer plans to combine payroll, attendance, health accommodation and collaboration-tool data to score employees for retention risk. The HR team cites Section 7's employment-related legitimate use as a blanket basis. The proposed model also uses optional wellness and location data that are not necessary for payroll or a documented employment purpose.
facts: The employer collects several categories of employee personal data for different purposes.
A proposed predictive score is a new use not explained in the existing employee notice.
The team has not identified which specific Section 7 condition supports each processing activity.
Access to health accommodation data is broader than necessary.
Employment status does not remove the need to test purpose, scope, safeguards and other applicable employment/sectoral law.
legal_issues: Section 7(i): specified employment purposes and purposes related to safeguarding the employer from loss or liability, within the clause's stated scope.
Sections 4 and 8: lawful-purpose analysis and Data Fiduciary duties, including security, retention and accountability.
Section 5: notice obligations apply according to the notified text and commencement.
Do not treat Section 7 as a general employer-interest exemption or as blanket permission for unrelated profiling.
penalty_analysis: Act Schedule, entry 7
Any other established contravention of the Act, such as an applicable notice or general duty
Up to ₹50 crore
No automatic penalty for using HR data; identify the specific provision, purpose and commencement. Other employment/privacy obligations require separate analysis.
remediation: Create a purpose-by-purpose HR data inventory and document the exact Section 7 condition, if any, for each activity.
Separate payroll/benefits processing from optional wellness, location and predictive analytics.
Perform a necessity and proportionality review before deploying employee scoring; assess bias, access, retention and effects on workers.
Restrict health accommodation data to a small authorised group and prevent its reuse for unrelated performance decisions.
Update clear employee notices where required and provide an appropriate contact and grievance route.
Review employment, labour, health and sector-specific obligations independently; retain the decision and control evidence.
cases.remediation_strategy: Require HR, privacy, security and employment counsel to approve each distinct purpose. Treat the Section 7 employment clause as bounded by its actual text and facts, not as a blanket consent substitute.
questions: Why is the employer's general business interest not enough by itself to invoke Section 7?
Which data categories and access groups should be separated?
What additional assessment is needed before using HR data for predictive scoring?
